name: Amira Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work from home three days a week for Kite, an online insurer that does pet and travel cover, and two days at the office by the river. My queue is mostly vet bills: a dog that ate a sock, a cat with a thyroid problem, a rabbit nobody knew was ill. I check the invoice against the policy, look for pre-existing conditions in the vet history, and pay or query it. I love the animals bit, honestly, and the photos people send.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The medical side. I left school at eighteen and I'm still learning what half the vet terms mean, so I miss things a more experienced person wouldn't, like a limp noted two years ago that makes a knee claim a pre-existing condition. I use AI tools every day to translate the vet notes into plain words and to draft queries, and my team leader Kwame is half impressed and half nervous about it. I share a flat in a housing co-op with three friends, so my rent's low and I've saved about a year of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say honestly that I'm a bit disappointed. I'd post something like: the tools are useful, but the hype was about making a few people rich, and it didn't even work. I'd still be the person on the team showing others how to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing, and that's fine. My job's safe, my rent's low, and there are loads of insurers in the city if Kite goes wrong. My real problem in that world is that I'm still not very good at the medical side yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and use the time the tools save to actually learn the vet stuff. Kwame's offered to pay for a short animal health course, and I'd do it next spring. I'd keep saving and maybe put a bit more into the index fund I started last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe, if I'm honest about how I feel about the future being dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools save time. How much, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good day maybe an hour, because I don't have to look up every word in a vet's notes. On a bad day the AI tool gets a drug name wrong and I lose the hour checking it. So it evens out more than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about, even in this quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette, who's been on the travel side for years and hates the new screens. Every time the system updates she has to relearn it, and she's started saying she'll retire early. Even a small change lands hardest on people like her.

say: I'd admit I'm a bit **disappointed** that the hype fizzled.
I'd post that the hype was about making **a few people rich**.
think: My job is **safe**, my rent is low, and other insurers are nearby.
My real problem is that I'm still **weak** on the **medical side**.
do: Take the **animal health course** Kwame offered next spring.
Use time saved by AI to **learn vet terms** properly.
Put a bit more into her **index fund**.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by a dull future.
S0.quote: On a bad day the AI tool gets a drug name wrong and I lose the hour checking it.
fieldNote: Amira is the one person who'd feel **let down** by AI stalling.
Her calm comes from **low co-op rent**, a year of savings and plenty of insurers nearby.
She notices that even small changes land hardest on **older colleagues** who hate new screens.

steps.text: Keep paying and querying vet bills for Kite from home
Take the short animal health course next spring
Put a bit more each month into her index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to organise, not to panic. The tools can make the job better if workers have a say in how they're used, and worse if we don't. I'd be posting about the union and about the people who don't use the tools getting left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm one of the people who comes out of this fine, at least for a few years. I already use the tools all day, so I'd be the one checking what the AI pays out. The thing that bothers me is that I'm good at the tool and still weak at the actual insurance, and that won't last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the automation project the week it's announced, and learn the workflow software properly, the stuff that sets rules for which claims a person sees. I'd keep doing the animal health course so I actually understand what I'm checking. And I'd get the union to push for a deal where people like Bernadette get proper training, not a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. I feel guilty about that, because I know some of the team will lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deal you'd want for Bernadette?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time to learn, with a real person teaching, and a promise she can't be let go during the first year while she's learning. And if she does want to retire early, a decent package. She's given that firm fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're good at the tool and weak at the insurance. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because once the tool gets better, the person checking it needs to know more than the tool, not less. Right now I'm a fast junior with a good gadget. In five years, being a fast junior with a good gadget isn't a job.

say: I'd say it's time to **organise**, not to panic.
Tools can make the job better if **workers have a say** in how they're used.
think: I'd probably come out **fine** for a **few years**, checking what the AI pays out.
I'm good at the tool but **weak at insurance**, and that gap won't last.
do: Volunteer for the **automation project** the week it's announced.
Learn the **workflow software** that decides which claims a person sees.
Push the union for **real training** for older colleagues like Bernadette.
feel: **Guilty** that she may do well while teammates lose out.
S1.quote: Right now I'm a fast junior with a good gadget. In five years, being a fast junior with a good gadget isn't a job.
fieldNote: Amira sees a **personal opening** in this picture, unlike most of her team.
She sharply notes that a checker must know **more than the tool**, and she doesn't yet.
Her progressive views show in a detailed **protection deal** for an older colleague.

steps.text: Volunteer for Kite's claims automation project the week it starts
Finish the animal health course to understand the claims she checks
Push the union for paid, in-person training for older staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs to be treated like a public emergency, and the gains have to be shared, through a tax on AI companies and some kind of basic income. I'd go to the marches. I'd also say, because it's true, that I use these tools and I'm still scared of this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My clerk job goes, I'm sure of that, probably by 2028. For a year or two someone needs to watch the AI, and I'd fight hard to be that someone, but that's a small number of seats. After that I need to be doing something with my hands before the robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd apply to whatever team is supervising the AI claims, and use that wage to pay for an electrician's apprenticeship in the evenings. Electricians will be busy wiring all the data centres and robot charging bays for a while. I'd also keep my year of savings untouched and stop topping up the index fund, because I'd want cash, not shares, in a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got a plan and no one depending on me, so it's the busy kind of anxious, not the frozen kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrician, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle does it, and he's never short of work. It's hands-on, so it buys about three years after the thinking AI, and somebody has to install everything the AI world runs on. It's not my dream, but it's a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go to the marches but also take a job supervising the AI. Do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not neatly, no. But marching doesn't pay rent, and I'd rather be inside the room seeing how the decisions get made. I'd tell the marchers what I see.

say: I'd call it a **public emergency** needing a tax on AI firms and **basic income**.
I'd admit that I use these tools and I'm **still scared** of this one.
think: My clerk job **goes by 2028**, and AI-watching seats are few.
I need **hands-on work** before the robots arrive around 2031.
do: Apply to the team **supervising AI claims** straight away.
Start an **electrician's apprenticeship** in the evenings, paid from that wage.
Stop topping up the **index fund** and keep a year of savings in cash.
feel: **Busy anxious**, not frozen, because she has a plan and no dependants.
S2.quote: Electricians will be busy wiring all the data centres and robot charging bays for a while.
fieldNote: Amira uses the **robot gap** cleanly: supervise AI now, wire buildings until 2031.
She sees the **tension** between marching and taking an AI-supervision job, and owns it.
Her **lack of dependants** is central to why she stays anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Apply to Kite's AI claims supervision team straight away
Start an evening electrician's apprenticeship with her uncle's help
Stop index fund top-ups and keep a year of costs in cash
Join marches for a tax on AI firms and basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for governments to set rules, and I'd be campaigning for them: limits on firing people for AI without notice, and money for retraining. I'd be loud about it online. I'd also keep showing people at work how to use the tools while they still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got time to get really good at something before the clerk job goes around 2030. I could be the best AI checker on the team for three or four years and save hard. Then I'd still want a trade for when the robots come, around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get myself onto the AI supervision team in the first year and take a part-time course in data and AI rules. I'd save half my wage, which I can do on co-op rent. And I'd start the electrician apprenticeship in 2029, while I've still got a wage to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sometimes a bit thrilled. I like having time to be clever about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half your wage? What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly, because I live cheaply already. Maybe the city break with my friends each spring, and takeaway Fridays. I'd rather go to the beach in a tent and have the money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmates about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to pick something now. One of them is a translator and she's already losing work, so she knows. The other two think it's all hype, and I'd keep pestering them.

say: I'd campaign for **notice rules** on AI firings and money for **retraining**.
I'd keep showing coworkers how to use the **tools** while they still can.
think: I've got time to become the **best AI checker** on the team before 2030.
I'd still want a **trade** for when robots come, around 2034.
do: Join the **AI supervision team** in the first year.
Take a part-time course in **AI rules** and save half her wage.
Start the **electrician apprenticeship** in 2029 while still earning.
feel: **Uneasy**, sometimes a bit **thrilled** at having time to plan cleverly.
S3.quote: I'd rather go to the beach in a tent and have the money in the bank.
fieldNote: Five years lets Amira **stack** her plans: AI checker first, then a trade.
Her **cheap co-op life** lets her save half her wage with little sacrifice.
She pesters friends who think it's **all hype**, showing her habit of moving early.

steps.text: Join Kite's AI supervision team within the first year
Start an electrician apprenticeship in 2029 while still earning
Save half her wage by cutting city breaks and takeaways
Campaign online for notice rules on AI-driven firings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get this right if we start now, and I'd push for it: a shorter week, free retraining, a share of the profits for everyone. I'd be hopeful in public, because I actually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives, with ten years of savings and skills. That's a good position. I think I'd actually like the job that comes after, whatever it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kite and grow into the AI side, maybe a claims automation analyst, over four or five years. Around 2030 I'd train as a vet nurse, because I've loved the animal side since day one and it's hands-on. I'd keep putting money in the index fund, because over ten years that's where it grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Properly calm, even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A vet nurse? Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the person who holds the dog while the vet works, puts in the drip, does the aftercare. I read a hundred vet notes a week and I keep thinking I'd rather be in the room with the dog. With ten years, I could do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this one go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the gains all go to a handful of companies and everyone else is fighting over scraps. Then it doesn't matter how well I plan. That's why I'd keep campaigning, even in the good version.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if we **start now**.
I'd push for a **shorter week**, free retraining and shared profits.
think: I'd be **37** with a decade of savings and skills when thinking AI arrives.
I'd probably **like the job** that comes after, whatever it is.
do: Grow into a **claims automation analyst** role at Kite over four or five years.
Keep adding to the **index fund** over the decade.
S4.quote: I read a hundred vet notes a week and I keep thinking I'd rather be in the room with the dog.
fieldNote: With a decade, Amira sees the change as **good for her** and plans two careers.
Her love of animals turns into a **hands-on goal** as a vet nurse.
Her one fear is **gains concentrating** in a few firms, which keeps her campaigning.

steps.text: Grow into a claims automation analyst role at Kite
Train as a vet nurse starting around 2030
Keep adding monthly to her index fund
Campaign for a shorter working week and shared AI profits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, not for me so much as for people like Bernadette, who'd have no time at all. For me, what would help is cheap evening training in trades, and a basic income so people can retrain without losing their homes. And clear rules, so firms can't just switch the lights off on a team overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the tools. I use AI tools every day, and I like them, but none of the money from them comes to the people whose work they learned from. That's the bit that actually makes me angry.

headlineQuote: I use AI tools every day, and I like them, but none of the money from them comes to the people whose work they learned from.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old pet claims clerk** at an online insurer, still weak on vet terms.
She uses **AI tools daily** and lives cheaply in a housing co-op with a year saved.
Progressive, she wants **shared gains** and union protection for colleagues slower to adapt.
She plans to supervise AI, then move into **hands-on work** as an electrician or vet nurse.
Her mood stays **calm to anxious**, never alarmed, thanks to savings and no dependants.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for colleagues like Bernadette who would have no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap evening **trade training** and a **basic income** during retraining.
**Clear rules** stopping firms from cutting whole teams overnight.
